name: Percona Operators
license: Apache 2.0 (operators). The databases they deploy keep their own licences: Percona Server for MongoDB is source-available under the SSPL
summary: Four free Kubernetes operators from Percona that run its builds of MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB, each using the engine’s own replication and backup tools.
intro: Percona has sold support for open-source databases since 2006 and publishes its own free builds of them: Percona Server for MySQL, Percona XtraDB Cluster, Percona Server for MongoDB and Percona Distribution for PostgreSQL, plus tools such as Percona XtraBackup and Percona Monitoring and Management (PMM). Its operators run those builds on Kubernetes. There is one per engine, each with its own custom resource and release cycle. The Operator for MySQL based on Percona XtraDB Cluster runs Galera synchronous replication, where every node takes writes and every write is confirmed by all nodes, so Percona recommends three to five nodes and an odd number; HAProxy or ProxySQL sits in front. The Operator for MySQL based on Percona Server runs MySQL Group Replication behind HAProxy or MySQL Router (generally available since 1.0.0 in November 2025), with asynchronous replication managed by Orchestrator still a tech preview.

The Operator for PostgreSQL is based on Crunchy Data’s PGO, so it uses Patroni for failover, pgBackRest for backups and PgBouncer for pooling; version 3.0 (May 2026) moved PGO’s resources to Percona’s own API group so the two operators can run side by side, and Percona documents a migration from PGO. The Operator for MongoDB runs replica sets and sharded clusters and backs them up with Percona Backup for MongoDB, whose agent runs beside each `mongod` and supports physical, incremental and snapshot backups with point-in-time recovery. The XtraDB Cluster operator backs up with XtraBackup to S3, Azure, Google Cloud Storage or a volume, and can upload binary logs every minute or so for point-in-time recovery. All four are Apache 2.0, Percona charges no licence fees for them or its images, and PMM can monitor them through a sidecar. Percona Everest, its web console on top of the operators, became the independent OpenEverest project in January 2026 and joined the CNCF Sandbox that March.
strengths: One vendor and one style of operator across MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB, with Apache 2.0 code and no licence fees for the images, unlike Crunchy’s PGO images
Each operator builds on the engine’s own machinery: Galera or Group Replication, Patroni, MongoDB replica sets and sharding, and XtraBackup, pgBackRest or Percona Backup for MongoDB
Monitoring through PMM, and a web console (OpenEverest) for teams who want self-service databases without writing YAML
A documented path from Crunchy’s PGO, since the PostgreSQL operator shares its design
limits: Four separate operators with different resources, release cycles and maturity: the Percona Server for MySQL operator only reached GA in late 2025, and its asynchronous mode is still a tech preview
They deploy Percona’s distributions rather than upstream images, and Percona Server for MongoDB inherits MongoDB’s source-available SSPL licence
XtraDB Cluster’s synchronous replication adds latency to every write, and Percona advises against more than five nodes because each one adds more
The operators are steered by one company and aren’t in a foundation; only the OpenEverest console has moved to the CNCF

story: Peter Zaitsev and Vadim Tkachenko started Percona in 2006 to support MySQL. It went on to publish its own open builds and tools: XtraBackup for hot MySQL backups in 2009, Percona Server for MySQL in 2010, Percona XtraDB Cluster in 2012, Percona Server for MongoDB in 2015, and PostgreSQL support from 2018. Its business is support and services, so the software itself stays free.

As customers moved applications to Kubernetes, they wanted the databases there too. In 2019 Percona launched its Kubernetes operators: version 1.0.0 of the XtraDB Cluster and MongoDB operators both shipped on May 29, 2019. A PostgreSQL operator followed in 2021, built on Crunchy Data’s open-source PGO instead of from scratch, and an operator for Percona Server for MySQL with Group Replication, started the same year, reached general availability in November 2025.

By 2024 Percona was promoting Everest, a web console that provisions databases through these operators on any Kubernetes cluster. In January 2026 Percona handed it to an independent, multi-vendor project called OpenEverest, which the CNCF accepted into its Sandbox on March 15, 2026. That May the PostgreSQL operator’s 3.0 release renamed the resources it had inherited from PGO, so Percona’s and Crunchy’s operators can share a cluster and users can migrate between them.

choices.why: MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB replicate and fail over in very different ways, so each operator wraps the engine’s own mechanism (Galera, Group Replication, Patroni, replica sets) instead of forcing one model on all three.

choices.choice: Build the PostgreSQL operator on PGO
choices.why: Crunchy’s Apache-licensed operator already combined Patroni and pgBackRest, so Percona reused it and later renamed the inherited APIs to avoid clashing with PGO.

choices.choice: Back up with each engine’s own tool
choices.why: XtraBackup, pgBackRest and Percona Backup for MongoDB already handle consistent physical backups and point-in-time recovery, and Percona maintains two of them.

choices.choice: Free images as well as free code
choices.why: Percona makes money from support and services, and markets the operators as having no licence fees or lock-in, in contrast to vendors that restrict their production images.
